name: AI Designed Drugs in Clinical Trials
blurb: How far AI derived candidates have progressed.
title: AI Designed Drugs in Clinical Trials
answer: Dozens of companies now have AI derived candidates in human trials, but most are early. An analysis presented at ASCO in 2026 found candidates from 63 companies in interventional trials, with 60 having completed phase 1 and only 8 phase 2. The first late stage trials, including a phase 3 for a generatively engineered antibody, began in late 2025.

reading.body:
AI has compressed the time to first human trials, not yet the time to approval. Of 63 companies with AI derived candidates in interventional trials, 60 have completed phase 1 and only 8 have reached phase 2.

The pipeline is wide at the base and narrow above it. That shape is normal for drug development, so the count alone does not prove AI candidates fail more often than conventional ones. What it does show is that the field has not yet accumulated enough phase 2 and phase 3 outcomes to make that comparison. The first late stage test, a phase 3 for a generatively engineered antibody, began in late 2025, and Rentosertib's phase 2a results were published in mid 2025. Those are the leading edge, not the body of evidence.

For AI specifically, the constraint has moved. Design and candidate generation are no longer the scarce step, which is why so many programs reached phase 1. The scarce step is now clinical validation, and that is gated by patient enrollment, trial site capacity, and years of follow up, none of which compute accelerates. A model that proposes molecules faster does not shorten a phase 3.

The data covers trial counts and two named readouts. It does not report success rates, effect sizes, or how these candidates compare with conventionally derived ones, so no claim about AI improving the odds of approval follows from it.

explainer:
Drug development normally loses most candidates along the way: many that enter phase 1 never reach approval, and phase 2, where a drug must first show it works in patients, is where most fail. AI companies claim two benefits, reaching the clinic faster and picking candidates more likely to succeed. The first is now well supported; several AI derived candidates moved from programme start to first human dosing in far less time than usual.

The second is not yet proven. Most AI derived candidates are still in phase 1 or early phase 2, the stages where few drugs have historically failed for lack of efficacy, so their apparent success rates are not comparable with industry averages yet. The decisive evidence will come from phase 2 and phase 3 results over the next few years, including the first late stage trials of generatively engineered antibodies and AI discovered small molecules.

How to count AI designed drugs

The phrase covers very different things. A molecule may have been designed by a generative model, or selected from a library by a model, or aimed at a target a model identified, or simply optimised with machine learning in the last step of medicinal chemistry. Published counts of AI designed drugs in trials vary by which of these definitions is used, and companies have an incentive to use the broadest. Reading any tally requires asking what AI actually did.

What the trial record shows

Several dozen candidates with a substantial AI contribution have entered clinical trials since about 2020, concentrated in oncology, fibrosis, inflammation and neuroscience. Some have reported positive early results; some have been discontinued, including a few that were widely publicised at entry. Analyses of early phase success rates have suggested AI derived candidates pass phase 1 at least as often as conventional ones, with too few phase 2 and 3 results to judge the later stages, which is where most drugs fail and where the real question lies.

What it means

AI has clearly shortened the discovery phase for some programmes and widened the chemistry companies can explore. Whether it improves the odds of success in late trials, which depends on choosing the right target and understanding the disease, is unproven and may remain so for years, because trials take that long. The honest position is that AI designed drugs are now a normal part of the industry pipeline, that they face the same trials as everything else, and that the next few years of phase 2 and 3 results will decide how much the method changes the economics of making medicines.
